function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow that will build the image and push it to GitHub Container Registry whenever you push to `main`.  

> **NOTE** – I’m not able to actually clone the repo or push changes for you, but the instructions below will get you up and running in minutes.

---

## 1. Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Add the following files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why Node 18?*  
> The repo is a Node.js project, so we use the official Node image.  
> If you prefer a different Node version, just change the `FROM` line.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s/` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *What this does:*  
> * **Deployment** – runs 2 replicas of your app.  
> * **Service** – exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster, forwarding to container port 3000.  
> * **Image** – points to the image that will be built/pushed by GitHub Actions (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> Adjust the image name/tag if you’re using a different registry.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file named `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest .

      # Push the image to GHCR
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> *How it works:*  
> 1. **Checkout** – pulls the repo.  
> 2. **Login** – authenticates to GHCR using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> 3. **Build** – builds the image from the Dockerfile.  
> 4. **Push** – pushes the image to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  

> **Tip:** If you want to use Docker Hub instead, replace the registry and credentials accordingly.

---

## 3. Add, Commit, and Push

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow, build the Docker image, and push it to GHCR. You can then deploy the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

---

## 4. Verify Everything

1. **Check the Actions tab** in GitHub to confirm the workflow ran successfully.  
2. **Verify the image** in GHCR: <https://github.com/zelarhq/packages/container/package/nodejs-welcome>  
3. **Deploy to Kubernetes** (if you have a cluster configured) and ensure the pods are running:

```bash
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
```

---

### Recap

| Step | What you did |
|------|--------------|
| 1 | Cloned the repo |
| 2 | Added Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow |
| 3 | Staged, committed, and pushed the changes |
| 4 | Verified the CI pipeline and deployed to Kubernetes |

You’re now set up with a fully automated build pipeline and ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes configuration! 🚀
